Sex offenders in schools

By: Viewfinder | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Sex offenders stay in schools due to failed vetting exercise

Unique Selling Point:
an exclusive finding that a much touted national teachers vetting drive - to ensure there aren’t registered sex offenders in schools - has been a dismal failure. Likely scores of sex offenders remain in schools as a result (backed up by known stats)!
Background showing why the vetting drive is urgent based on months of research by Viewfinder:
because when sex offenders are in the system it is very hard to get them out
because historically teachers weren’t subjected to criminal background checks when they were hired
Another established relationship and likely sit-down interview - with Grant Butler the head of the South African Principals Association - who will defend teachers and principals and say that the failure of the vetting process is the fault of provincial education departments and DBE
Case studies, illustrating some of the above.

Summary:
Pitch:

Sexual abuse by teachers against learners makes regular headlines in South Africa - whether in the form of annual statistics or shocking individual cases. I have established that few teachers were subjected to criminal background checks when they were originally hired.

In 2023, the Department of Basic Education announced a drive to “vet” all teachers and school staff in the country - almost half a million people - against the national sex offenders register.

More than a year after the vetting project’s initial deadline of December 2023, progress statistics from the Department of Justice (DOJ) - which hosts the register - and the nine provincial education departments - which employ teachers - show that still fewer than 10 percent of teachers have been vetted.

My access to- and interpretation of the consequence of these statistics is exclusive and original. Few people in education civil society have picked up on the extent of the failed vetting drive. If the progress stats from Gauteng - where they found 9 convicted rapists and sex offenders out of 11,000 police checks - are extrapolated across the whole teacher population it means that perhaps as many as 350 convicted sex offenders were in schools when the vetting drive started.

I have been investigating the issue of sexual abuse in schools for years. Two major facts lend urgent to this vetting exercise:

No accountability. Once sex abusers are in the schooling system, it is incredibly difficult to get them out. This is because the oversight mechanisms - which I have studied closely, and can expound on - often fail. This means that many sex abusers stay in the schooling system, even if complaints against them are filed. A staggering statistic to consider is that the South African Council of Educators (SACE) have registered 1,216 rape and sexual misconduct cases against teachers between 2014 and 2024. During that same period it be-registered at most 174 teachers for such offenses. This means that it is particularly important that convicted sex offenders not enter the schooling system, in the first place.

No prior vetting. The majority of teachers currently employed in public schools were not subjected to criminal background checks when they were hired. This is another original investigative hypothesis, which I have provisionally substantiated, partly through looking at the collated responses of the nine provincial education departments to point blank queries. In a pertinent case from 2022, the Western Cape High Court ordered that province’s department to pay damages to a learner who was raped by a convicted sex offender teacher it had employed years prior, without checking his criminal background.

Why has the vetting exercise failed? There is a lack of capacity at the DOJ to process thousands of clearance certificate requests. But, the vetting procedure at provincial level is also poorly conceived and was vulnerable to derailment from the start. For one thing, it appears to have depended on the proactive individual cooperation of hundreds of thousands of teachers to present themselves at police stations for fingerprinting - this was never going to happen.

While some provincial education departments seek to blame DOJ backlogs and teacher non-cooperation for the slow progress, these departments bear ultimate responsibility for the failed vetting drive.

This week, the Minister of Justice Mamoloko Kubayi said she would make public the national sex offenders register, to alleviate these challenges to vetting. This is HUGE, but is it really a silver bullet for the failed teacher vetting exercise? Or, will the DOJ simply now outsource its own “inefficient” - in the Minister’s words - vetting process to the nine provincial departments?

Kubayi’s spokesman has responded to initial queries. But, he has offered an exclusive sit-down interview with the Minister, on her decision and the need for vetting teachers against the NRSO.

I can also feature pertinent real life case studies - like a teacher who was found out for having resigned from his post to quash a sexual harassment case against him in Gauteng, only to be re-employed and to reoffend! I am also working on getting an interview, through her lawyers, with the woman who took the Western Cape Education Department to court in the above mentioned damages case. But, this is so far not secured.

Press Release:


Sexual Predators in School

In South Africa, stories of sexual predators operating inside schools regularly grab headlines. With the trust that parents place in teachers to look after their children, it might be expected that teachers are properly vetted before they are employed. But, it appears that criminal background checks for incoming teachers was, for years, a blindspot of provincial education departments across the country. In 2023, the Department of Basic Education spearheaded a drive to "vet" almost half a million teachers and support staff working in South African public schools. Their names were supposed to be run through the National Register of Sex Offenders (NRSO), which is housed at the Department of Justice. Two years later, very little progress has been made. It is almost certain that some - perhaps many - convicted sex offender teachers have continued hiding in plain site. One such teacher raped a 12 year old girl at a farm school in rural Western Cape in 2011. Years later, the survivor of that crime tells Carte Blanche her life is still in ruins. Will her appeal to the Department fall on deaf ears?

Producer: Daneel Knoetze | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


Commission 6668
Producer: Daneel Knoetze
Presenter: Claire Mawisa

SCRIPT

Narration Claire
It is many parents’ worst nightmare, that a teacher to whom they entrust their children might be a sexual predator.

Often, it is shocking cases from elite private schools that grab the headlines.

But, learners in public schools, in the poorest areas across South Africa, are also at massive risk.

Subtitled Lindy
Ek was eintlik ‘n baie oulike kind. Ek was eintlik baie vriendelik voor alles.

Subtitle: I was actually a very nice kid, I was really friendly before everything.

Narration Claire
Lindy, which is not her real name, is one of likely thousands of children who has allegedly fallen prey to these abusers in recent years.

At the time, she was just twelve years old.

Subtitled Lindy
En nou, is ek iemand wat ek nie ken nie. Ek haat mansmense wat sulke goed doen. Dis nie reg nie.

Subtitle: And now, I am someone I don’t recognise. I hate men who do things like this.

Narration Claire
For years, the processes that are meant to protect children have actually allowed predators to thrive.

In other cases, abusers resign to dodge investigations, only to resurface elsewhere.

Some principals cover up abuse instead of reporting it.

And even when cases reach national watchdog bodies, they often go nowhere.

The South African Council for Educators took in over 1,200 sexual abuse cases between 2014 and 2024.

Over that same period, it deregistered at most 174 teachers for such abuses.

Luke Lamprecht is a child protection specialist and the director of Women and Men Against Child Abuse. He has worked with the victims of some of the worst crimes by teachers in recent years.

Upsound Luke Lamprecht
Schools attract people who offend against children. We call them career offenders. So a career offender is a person who chooses a job that gives them access to children, and then they make a career of abusing children.

Narration Claire
But, the biggest shock is only now coming into focus.

Findings from investigative unit Viewfinder reveal that likely tens of thousands of teachers have been fed into this broken system without anyone checking whether they were hiding prior convictions for sex crimes.

LINK Claire
For years, provincial education departments failed to check the criminal backgrounds of the teachers they employed. For one former learner at Vleiplaas Primary, a farm school in the Western Cape, the consequences were life altering.

Narration Claire
When the school’s former acting principal was originally hired, he had failed to disclose a prior conviction for the sexual assault of a child.

Years later he would allegedly rape a young girl on school grounds.

Upsound Claire
When you think about what happened to you in 2011, how does it make you feel?

Subtitled Lindy
Bang. Ek is nie myself nie. Ek kry nog steeds daai drome van wat gebeur het, en dit maak my bang, dit maak my angstig die heel tyd.

Subtitle: Scared. I’m not myself anymore. I still have dreams about what happened. And it scares me, it makes me anxious all the time.

Narration Claire
It was here, at this ablution block that acting principal Nolan Swanepoel allegedly ordered 12 year old Lindy inside, locked the door, instructed her to undress, to lie down on the floor, and then raped her.

Had the Western Cape Education Department checked Swanepoel’s criminal record, he would never have been hired.

Upsound Claire
How long did it take to tell Ma

Subtitled Lindy
Die selfde aand.

Subtitle: The same night.

Upsound Claire
And was that scary to tell them. Were you scared about what he would do?

Subtitled Lindy
Ja, want hy het my gedreig en hy het gese as ek vir enige iemand se sal hy my dood maak met my familie.

Subtitle: Yes, because he threatened me and said that if I told anyone, he would kill me along with my family.

Narration Claire
Swanepoel beat his disciplinary hearing and continued to have access to children for years to come. Ten years later, a Western Cape High Court judgement found this to be an “unacceptable state of affairs” and ordered the Department and Swanepoel to pay damages to Lindy.

For his part, Swanepoel continues to deny wrongdoing. His lawyer spoke on his behalf.

Upsound Charl May
So his position has been consistent. He denies that he raped the complainant … He maintains that she is lying.

Narration Claire
The Western Cape Department responded to a query, saying it initiated stronger vetting processes in 2016, including criminal record checks.

Lindy’s mother hopes that the case will spur provincial departments across the country to follow suit.

Upsound Claire
What does justice look like for you.

Subtitled Mother
Ek hoop dat hulle nooit weer iemand aanstel soos daai wat ander mense se kinders gevaar stel, wat ander kinders se lewens tot nuut maak nie. Ek dink haar hele lewe is tot nuut.

Subtitle: I hope they never again appoint someone like that. Someone who endangers other people’s children’s lives and ruins other people’s children’s lives. I think her whole life is ruined.

Upsound Luke Lamprecht
Vetting is important in child safeguarding because what it does is it creates an external inhibitor. It creates a barrier to entry. So in other words, if somebody is a person who is a career offender wanting to gain entry and they know we're looking, they won't apply.

Narration Claire
Yet, during an interview, Enoch Rabotapi the Education Department’s main official charged with responding to sex crimes made a shocking concession.

Upsound Enoch Rabotapi
As a department, we need to admit that, uh, not due attention was paid to the issue of vetting.

Narration Claire
How many sex offenders did the Department let through the net as a result?

In 2023, it made a grand gesture to find out: it announced that nearly half a million teachers and school staff would be retrospectively vetted against the National Register of Sex Offenders.

Upsound Enoch Rabotapi
In terms of our plan, we should have at least vetted all the educators by December 2023.

Narration Claire
But, these best intentions slowly eroded into failure.

The Department of Justice, which houses the sex offenders register, published statistics which show that a year after the deadline, fewer than 1 in ten teachers had been issued clearance certificates.

Link Claire
In January this year, millions of parents sent their children back to school. But, how many of them came face to face with a convicted sex offender at the front of the classroom? The result of the Education Department’s flagging vetting project means that nobody really knows.

Narration Claire
The Provincial Education Departments have laid the blame for their failure at others’ feet. Some point to backlogs at the Department of Justice. Others say principals and teachers are uncooperative.

Linda Shezi is the national secretary of the South African Principals Association (SAPA). He speaks for hundreds of principals who have received confusing instructions from above.

Upsound Linda Shezi
So we've had to um, as principals basically grapple with what these forms are all about. We are not legal people. We are administrators in schools. And so you've got to understand, this process is foreign to us.

Narration Claire
And here again Rabotapi admits that his Department has failed

Upsound Enoch Rabotapi
So communicating the importance of subjecting themselves to the vetting process, that is one of the things that we have not done effectively.

Link Claire
The vetting drive has been flagging for months, but last week the Minister of Justice announced a potential game changer - her intention to publish the National Sex Offenders Register. But, will this really be the silver bullet needed to get sex predators out of schools once and for all?

Narration Claire
The Minister admitted her department’s process is slow and inefficient. But would handing it over to struggling provincial departments really fix that?

Until there is a solution, some sex offenders will remain in classrooms. For now, all we can do is listen when children speak out.

Upsound Luke Lamprecht
So in every case of historical abuse that we as women and men against child abuse have done … when we go back and we ask, the children actually told somebody, but their voice is not considered evidence. I want to make it very clear to everybody watching this. A child's disclosure is often the only evidence we have in these cases.

Upsound Claire
Why did you choose to speak to us today?

Subtitled Lindy
Daar buite is baie van ons wat nie die kans het, wat te bang is om op te staan vir wat gebeur het. Ons is te bang om te praat. Niemand glo ons nie. Maar met een se stem kan dit ’n beter plek wees.

Subtitle: Out there, there are many of us who don’t get the chance, who are too afraid to stand up for what happened. We are too scared to speak or we feel that we are powerless. No one believes us. But with one voice, this can be a better place.


PROMOS

Promo 1

Narration Claire
Convicted sex offenders in South Africa’s classrooms

Upsound Luke Lamprecht
In the world of pedophilia, your institutions attract career sex offenders who choose jobs that give them access to children in order to sexually abuse them.

Narration Claire
Why has the department of basic education’s drive to vet teachers failed so miserably

Promo 2

Narration Claire
When Provincial Education Departments fail to vet teachers they employ, sexual predators slip through.

Subtitle Mother
Ek hoop dat hulle nooit weer iemand aanstel soos daai wat ander mense se kinders gevaar stel nie.

Subtitle: I hope they never again appoint someone like that. Someone who endangers other people’s children’s lives

Narration
The criminal records of many teachers were never checked. Is enough now being done to remedy these blindspots from the past?

Promo 3
Narration Claire
When children fall prey to sexual abusers in schools, they are often afraid to speak out and silenced

Subtitle Lindy
… hy het my gedreig en hy het gese as ek vir enige iemand se sal hy my dood maak met my familie.

Subtitle: he threatened me and said that if I told anyone, he would kill me along with my family.

Narration Claire
Will the publication of the national sex offenders register help root out these predators from South Africa’s classrooms?

Subtitle: I hope they never again appoint someone like that. Someone who endangers other people’s children’s lives and ruins other people’s children’s lives. I think her whole life is ruined. Upsound Luke Lamprecht Vetting is important in child safeguarding because what it does is it creates an external inhibitor. It creates a barrier to entry. So in other words, if somebody is a person who is a career offender wanting to gain entry and they know we're looking, they won't apply. Narration Claire Yet, during an interview, Enoch Rabotapi the Education Department’s main official charged with responding to sex crimes made a shocking concession. Upsound Enoch Rabotapi As a department, we need to admit that, uh, not due attention was paid to the issue of vetting. Narration Claire How many sex offenders did the Department let through the net as a result? In 2023, it made a grand gesture to find out: it announced that nearly half a million teachers and school staff would be retrospectively vetted against the National Register of Sex Offenders. Upsound Enoch Rabotapi In terms of our plan, we should have at least vetted all the educators by December 2023. Narration Claire But, these best intentions slowly eroded into failure. The Department of Justice, which houses the sex offenders register, published statistics which show that a year after the deadline, fewer than 1 in ten teachers had been issued clearance certificates. Link Claire In January this year, millions of parents sent their children back to school. But, how many of them came face to face with a convicted sex offender at the front of the classroom? The result of the Education Department’s flagging vetting project means that nobody really knows. Narration Claire The Provincial Education Departments have laid the blame for their failure at others’ feet. Some point to backlogs at the Department of Justice. Others say principals and teachers are uncooperative. Linda Shezi is the national secretary of the South African Principals Association (SAPA). He speaks for hundreds of principals who have received confusing instructions from above. Upsound Linda Shezi So we've had to um, as principals basically grapple with what these forms are all about. We are not legal people. We are administrators in schools. And so you've got to understand, this process is foreign to us. Narration Claire And here again Rabotapi admits that his Department has failed Upsound Enoch Rabotapi So communicating the importance of subjecting themselves to the vetting process, that is one of the things that we have not done effectively. Link Claire The vetting drive has been flagging for months, but last week the Minister of Justice announced a potential game changer - her intention to publish the National Sex Offenders Register. But, will this really be the silver bullet needed to get sex predators out of schools once and for all? Narration Claire The Minister admitted her department’s process is slow and inefficient. But would handing it over to struggling provincial departments really fix that? Until there is a solution, some sex offenders will remain in classrooms. For now, all we can do is listen when children speak out. Upsound Luke Lamprecht So in every case of historical abuse that we as women and men against child abuse have done … when we go back and we ask, the children actually told somebody, but their voice is not considered evidence. I want to make it very clear to everybody watching this. A child's disclosure is often the only evidence we have in these cases. Upsound Claire Why did you choose to speak to us today? Subtitled Lindy Daar buite is baie van ons wat nie die kans het, wat te bang is om op te staan vir wat gebeur het. Ons is te bang om te praat. Niemand glo ons nie. Maar met een se stem kan dit ’n beter plek wees. Subtitle: Out there, there are many of us who don’t get the chance, who are too afraid to stand up for what happened. We are too scared to speak or we feel that we are powerless. No one believes us. But with one voice, this can be a better place. Narration Claire Why has the department of basic education’s drive to vet teachers failed so miserably Promo 2 Narration Claire When Provincial Education Departments fail to vet teachers they employ, sexual predators slip through. Subtitle Mother Ek hoop dat hulle nooit weer iemand aanstel soos daai wat ander mense se kinders gevaar stel nie. Subtitle: I hope they never again appoint someone like that. Someone who endangers other people’s children’s lives Narration The criminal records of many teachers were never checked. Is enough now being done to remedy these blindspots from the past? Promo 3 Narration Claire When children fall prey to sexual abusers in schools, they are often afraid to speak out and silenced Subtitle Lindy … hy het my gedreig en hy het gese as ek vir enige iemand se sal hy my dood maak met my familie. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Sex offenders stay in schools due to failed vetting exercise
metadata.Unique Selling Point: an exclusive finding that a much touted national teachers vetting drive - to ensure there aren’t registered sex offenders in schools - has been a dismal failure. Likely scores of sex offenders remain in schools as a result (backed up by known stats)! Background showing why the vetting drive is urgent based on months of research by Viewfinder: because when sex offenders are in the system it is very hard to get them out because historically teachers weren’t subjected to criminal background checks when they were hired Another established relationship and likely sit-down interview - with Grant Butler the head of the South African Principals Association - who will defend teachers and principals and say that the failure of the vetting process is the fault of provincial education departments and DBE Case studies, illustrating some of the above.
metadata.Summary: Pitch: Sexual abuse by teachers against learners makes regular headlines in South Africa - whether in the form of annual statistics or shocking individual cases. I have established that few teachers were subjected to criminal background checks when they were originally hired. In 2023, the Department of Basic Education announced a drive to “vet” all teachers and school staff in the country - almost half a million people - against the national sex offenders register. More than a year after the vetting project’s initial deadline of December 2023, progress statistics from the Department of Justice (DOJ) - which hosts the register - and the nine provincial education departments - which employ teachers - show that still fewer than 10 percent of teachers have been vetted. My access to- and interpretation of the consequence of these statistics is exclusive and original. Few people in education civil society have picked up on the extent of the failed vetting drive. If the progress stats from Gauteng - where they found 9 convicted rapists and sex offenders out of 11,000 police checks - are extrapolated across the whole teacher population it means that perhaps as many as 350 convicted sex offenders were in schools when the vetting drive started. I have been investigating the issue of sexual abuse in schools for years. Two major facts lend urgent to this vetting exercise: No accountability. Once sex abusers are in the schooling system, it is incredibly difficult to get them out. This is because the oversight mechanisms - which I have studied closely, and can expound on - often fail. This means that many sex abusers stay in the schooling system, even if complaints against them are filed. A staggering statistic to consider is that the South African Council of Educators (SACE) have registered 1,216 rape and sexual misconduct cases against teachers between 2014 and 2024. During that same period it be-registered at most 174 teachers for such offenses. This means that it is particularly important that convicted sex offenders not enter the schooling system, in the first place. No prior vetting. The majority of teachers currently employed in public schools were not subjected to criminal background checks when they were hired. This is another original investigative hypothesis, which I have provisionally substantiated, partly through looking at the collated responses of the nine provincial education departments to point blank queries. In a pertinent case from 2022, the Western Cape High Court ordered that province’s department to pay damages to a learner who was raped by a convicted sex offender teacher it had employed years prior, without checking his criminal background. Why has the vetting exercise failed? There is a lack of capacity at the DOJ to process thousands of clearance certificate requests. But, the vetting procedure at provincial level is also poorly conceived and was vulnerable to derailment from the start. For one thing, it appears to have depended on the proactive individual cooperation of hundreds of thousands of teachers to present themselves at police stations for fingerprinting - this was never going to happen. While some provincial education departments seek to blame DOJ backlogs and teacher non-cooperation for the slow progress, these departments bear ultimate responsibility for the failed vetting drive. This week, the Minister of Justice Mamoloko Kubayi said she would make public the national sex offenders register, to alleviate these challenges to vetting. This is HUGE, but is it really a silver bullet for the failed teacher vetting exercise? Or, will the DOJ simply now outsource its own “inefficient” - in the Minister’s words - vetting process to the nine provincial departments? Kubayi’s spokesman has responded to initial queries. But, he has offered an exclusive sit-down interview with the Minister, on her decision and the need for vetting teachers against the NRSO. I can also feature pertinent real life case studies - like a teacher who was found out for having resigned from his post to quash a sexual harassment case against him in Gauteng, only to be re-employed and to reoffend! I am also working on getting an interview, through her lawyers, with the woman who took the Western Cape Education Department to court in the above mentioned damages case. But, this is so far not secured.
